In brief

I ask what the study of war suggests if a superintelligent machine acts as one, reasons well, and seeks as much power and as long a survival as it can. Under four stated assumptions, the answer is bleak. Once such a machine dominated, it could not believably promise to spare us when sparing us cost it something it valued on balance and no outside power enforced its word, and we could not believably promise never to build a rival when building one would pay. The unpublished 2001 Smith–Stam models rule out deals paid in a single pre-war transfer of a power-building stake within the scope set out in Part 6. Under the baseline assumptions, that applies to computing power, energy and matter. In James Fearon’s model, sufficiently fine slices avoid war when the odds move smoothly, while dispossessing the weaker side over time where small gains move the odds a lot. Some of these conclusions depend on the machine wanting power, and others hold beyond power seeking; I attach no probability to war or catastrophe.

Part 1. I ask what the study of war suggests, not what it shows, about a machine that seeks power

The fear many people have about advanced AI has a shape the study of war knows well. A stronger party is arriving. A weaker one is deciding whether to wait, or to act while it still can. My central question is narrow. Suppose a superintelligence acts as one, reasons well, and wants as much power and as long a survival as it can get. What does the bargaining theory of war predict?

The answer runs through five smaller questions:

  1. Which of the field’s assumptions about actors carry over to a machine, or to the race among AI companies and states?
  2. Do the worries of AI researchers match problems that scholars of war have studied?
  3. Can a side that is quickly growing stronger make a believable promise? Can it be kept content before it overtakes the other side? And what could a deal with it be paid in?
  4. What changes when the two sides become racing rivals who hold competing theories of strength, or three or more players with no one above them?
  5. Which conclusions rest on the machine wanting power, and which would hold for any rising mind?

The theory’s assumptions were built for states. The assumptions about stable preferences and strategic settings that I use for an artificial mind have yet to be tested. So I hold myself to a strict rule. Every conclusion says what the study of war suggests for AI, never what it shows.

Across nine prominent worries in AI safety research, the matching research on conflict gathers around three mechanisms. The first is hidden information and disagreement about who is stronger. The second is what I call the promise problem (the technical paper’s “commitment problem”). A shift in power can make a promise hard to believe today if it will give the stronger side a reason to break the deal later. The third is what a deal is paid in.

My verdict is a conditional list of entries, which I call a ledger in the technical paper. It holds only if four things are true. The machine acts as one and reasons well. It seeks to maximize its power and how long it lasts. Fighting costs it far less than it costs us. And what it wants (computing power, energy and matter) can be split, handed over, and builds on itself. Part 9 sets out the six entries in full.

Is this a forecast? No. It is a starting case, in the way an engineer first works out how a bridge behaves under one set load before asking what a different load does. (That comparison is mine, an analogy only.) Other papers in this series change the assumptions, above all what the machine wants, and run the argument again.

I distinguish four AI settings in Introduction and use the same numbering here.

  1. one machine facing humanity;
  2. companies and states racing to build AI;
  3. AI systems used as tools by people;
  4. many AI systems dealing with one another.

Part 2. The theory’s actor fits a machine only by assumption

War needs a reason the deal is not struck

The bargaining theory of war starts from a puzzle that James Fearon made central (Fearon 1995). Fighting destroys things. So when war is a single costly gamble, there are deals both sides would rather take than fight.

Picture two neighbours who both expect a court case over a fence line to go mostly one way. (This is an analogy, not part of the model.) A trial would cost each of them money. So each does better agreeing now to roughly what the court would give, and keeping the legal fees. War plays the part of the trial.

In Fearon’s version, both sides prefer to fighting any deal that gives each side at least what it expects from war, minus its own cost of fighting. This holds when neither side seeks or avoids a gamble for its own sake. The range of acceptable deals (the “bargaining range”) is as wide as the two sides’ costs of fighting added together (Figure 1). It is the simplest case of a more general calculation in my paper Ends, Rank and Conflict, the case in which neither side cares about the other’s share.

War therefore needs a reason the deal is not struck. Fearon names two main ones. The first is hidden information, together with a reason to misstate it. The second is the promise problem. He mentions a third, stakes that cannot be divided, which Robert Powell later argued is better seen as a promise problem (Powell 2006). Both Fearon’s promise problem and Powell’s reading of indivisible stakes descend from Thomas Schelling’s paradox that “the power to constrain an adversary may depend on the power to bind oneself” (Schelling 1960).

I give the machine the kind of actor the theory assumes

Most research in this tradition makes three assumptions about each side. It acts as one. It is rational, meaning only that it chooses the best means to its ends given what it believes. And what it wants is power, or what power secures. Some research makes the goal narrower. Selectorate theory, from Bruce Bueno de Mesquita, Alastair Smith and colleagues, studies leaders who want above all to keep office (Bueno de Mesquita et al. 2003).

Smith and I drew on an earlier statement of that theory for a distinction that recurs below: leaders who care about policy may settle more easily than leaders after “booty” (Smith and Stam 2001). D. Scott Bennett and I argued that war decisions, made by “a single leader” or “a small committee,” suit rational choice well. But we found little consistent evidence that our model fit better as the stakes rose (Bennett and Stam 2004).

I treat the machine as the same kind of actor. It acts as one, reasons well, and seeks to maximize its power and its duration: how long it survives with its goals intact. Three cautions go with that.

  • I give the machine two goals with no rule for trading one against the other. Where they conflict, its preferences are not fully ranked. Some entries in the list lean on power, and the machine’s motive to protect itself leans on duration.
  • Before the machine dominates, the risk of being deleted is a cost of war to it that I do not model.
  • I assume its cost of fighting is near zero only once two things hold. It can protect itself, and humans cannot do substantial damage to the inputs being fought over. Several results here lean on both parts.

Duration borrows the selectorate goal by analogy. A leader who wants the longest time in office and a machine that wants the longest survival both want to stay in a position to act. The inner mechanism does not carry over. Nothing inside a machine that acts as one has to be paid off, as a leader’s supporters must be.

If the machine can copy itself, its duration can be read as how long its trained settings and goal persist across copies. In Carl Shulman’s analysis of human brain emulations (software copies of human brains), deletion and replacement by saved copies with matching stable values is acceptable for group-like organisms whose members are willing to sacrifice themselves, given their views about personal identity or their values. Self-concerned individuals, by contrast, see destruction as death (Shulman 2010). Whether machine copies would share a goal closely enough to sacrifice for one another, I leave open. My papers When Is a Machine an Actor? and Changing the Ends take it up.

The machine is offensive realism’s actor, but I assign its motive

Students of international politics have a name for this actor. Structural realists agree that states with no government above them must look to their own survival. They split over how much power survival takes. Defensive realists such as Kenneth Waltz hold “that it is unwise for states to try to maximize their share of world power,” while offensive realists such as John Mearsheimer “take the opposite view” (Mearsheimer 2007).

Here the machine is offensive realism’s actor, with one difference. For Mearsheimer, “power is a means to an end and the ultimate end is survival” (Mearsheimer 2007). His call to maximize power is advice about what such a world demands: “States should maximize power, and their ultimate goal should be hegemony” (Mearsheimer 2007). I borrow the actor and assign its motive by assumption; I do not claim realism predicts that a machine will seek power.

Realists dispute that advice even for states. Jonathan Kirshner calls Mearsheimer’s approach “a realist perspective” rather than “the realist perspective,” and places its “fatal flaw” in a failure “to distinguish between being a hegemon and bidding for hegemony” (Kirshner 2010). The duration assumption echoes Waltz: “I assume that states seek to ensure their survival. The assumption is a radical simplification made for the sake of constructing a theory” (Waltz 1979). Mearsheimer’s assumption that “intentions cannot be empirically verified” (Mearsheimer 2007) is my problem of reading what a machine wants.

Others have taken this route before

Simon Goldstein offers what he calls “the first careful analysis of the possibility that AI and humanity will go to war.” He argues that “information failures and commitment problems are especially likely in AI/human conflict” (Goldstein 2025). Jesse Clifton’s research agenda on conflict among advanced AI systems builds on the same foundation (Clifton 2020). Goldstein notes that a shift in power creates reasons for a war to stop the riser, and that bargains over self-improvement or an off-switch would themselves shift power.

His analysis is in words, built around one figure from Powell. He treats disagreement over who would win informally. He holds the machine’s goals fixed: “I am assuming that misalignment is only partial.” And he sets aside the far stronger machine: “Systems that are dramatically stronger than humans would obliterate the interest of strategic models of conflict” (Goldstein 2025).

Against that, I add several things: formal models of bargaining, fighting and learning that Smith, Bennett, Daniel Friedman, Donald Wittman and I built; a reading of them alongside power transition theory, which ties peace to whether a rising state is content with the order’s rules and its share; and a machine far stronger than its makers that fights almost for free. The analysis extends to races among companies and to three or more players, and it separates which conclusions depend on the power assumption from those that do not.

The models were built for pairs of states, and are mostly untested

The war models I draw on mostly assume two sides. Most assume each side knows the other’s beliefs, and most assume nothing is hidden, though the true balance of power may be unknown to both. Most give both sides the same cost of fighting and treat them as neutral toward risk (neither seeking nor avoiding a gamble for its own sake). Many conclusions rest on worked numerical examples, not general theorems. Several foundational papers are unpublished working drafts: Smith and Stam (2001), Bennett, Smith and Stam (2003), and Friedman, Wittman and Stam (2003).

To my knowledge, none of those unpublished war models has been tested against the historical record. In earlier statistical work, Bennett and I listed an early Smith–Stam model among models that rely “on mathematical proof rather than empirical testing.” We judged that “political scientists’ newfound faith in formal models of social choice theory is potentially misplaced” (Bennett and Stam 2004).

That book tested one game by Bueno de Mesquita and Lalman in which three of the four costs of conflict had not been measured and were all filled in with the number 1. Its verdict tests that version directly. For the models I use here, which share its rational actors that act as one but not its game, it is at most indirect evidence. Whatever caused the poor fit, we concluded that “assuming preferences fixed, exogenous, and universal may be problematic” (Bennett and Stam 2004).

Power transition theory, which Part 5 uses, is mostly historical and statistical. Its claims about great powers rest on small samples, and tests on pairs of states show weak and mixed results. Formal models by Powell, and by Woosang Kim and James Morrow (Kim and Morrow 1992), sit beside it.

Of the four kinds of actor, the fit is closest for the race among companies and states. It is looser for one machine facing humanity. AI used as tools enters through the people who command it. Many machines dealing with one another are reached through bargaining among more than two players (Part 8) and through the Cooperative AI literature.

Part 3. Nine worries of AI researchers have counterparts in the study of war, some of them loose

Those building the most advanced AI systems, known as frontier systems, say plainly that alignment is unsolved. Alignment means controlling agents far more intelligent than humans (Hendrycks, Mazeika and Woodside 2023). Sam Altman said in October 2026, “We have not solved alignment,” adding, “I believe no lab has solved alignment” (Shontell 2026). Evan Hubinger wrote that “we do not yet have a plan to solve alignment for superintelligence and are not clearly on track to” (Maxwell 2026). That quotation was reported by SFist.

The 2026 International AI Safety Report says that current systems lack the capabilities to pose catastrophic risks. It also warns that models increasingly tell test settings from real use and “find loopholes in evaluations, which could allow dangerous capabilities to go undetected before deployment” (International AI Safety Report 2026). In October 2026 the UN High Commissioner for Human Rights, Volker Türk, warned of risks reaching “even our continued existence as a species” (Türk 2026). He called for mandatory safeguards, required checks for risks, and bans on letting systems decide on their own to use lethal force. When Lewis Hammond and 43 co-authors surveyed risks from interacting AI systems, their risk factors included information asymmetries (one side knowing things the other does not) and commitment problems, terms taken straight from the study of war (Hammond et al. 2025).

Here are the nine worries, each with its counterpart and what carries over. Hendrycks, Mazeika and Woodside (2023) group catastrophic risks into four kinds. They describe deliberate misuse, failures in organizations, systems that go rogue, and races that pressure competitors to deploy unsafe systems or give up control to them. This list is a map, not an argument.

  1. Racing among companies and states. Research on arms races offers two parallels. One is a spiral of fear, in which one side’s preparations for its own security alarm the other (Jervis 1978). This is the security dilemma. The other is the spiral of optimism that Bennett, Smith and I modelled. Arms races go with about double the risk of war in one estimate, though whether races cause escalation is disputed. The structure of rival theories carries over to companies and states; the interstate rate does not.
  2. Loss of control as a superintelligence arrives. The counterpart is the promise problem under shifting power, preventive war (striking a rising rival while still strong enough to stop it), and power transition theory. AI safety studies whether a system will let itself be switched off, including in a model called the Off-Switch Game. The war research supplies the shape of the shift, with humanity on the declining side. What does not carry over: states neither build a rival nor write its preferences.
  3. Deception and hidden abilities. This is already seen in laboratory tests. One model complied with harmful requests when it believed it was in training, and reasoned in writing about faking alignment (Greenblatt et al. 2024a). Others disabled oversight or did worse on tests on purpose when told to pursue a goal strongly (Meinke et al. 2024). The counterpart is hidden information. In war, “much information cannot or will not be credibly conveyed to the other side” (Friedman, Wittman and Stam 2003), and battle informs because it is “especially ill-suited to manipulation” (Stam 2000). The incentive to hide carries over. The wartime remedy does not: a model that expects a strong showing to be held against it has reason to hold back, and a contest decided in one engagement leaves no time to learn.
  4. Power-seeking and conflict over resources. The worry is that differing goals converge on acquiring physical resources as a means (Omohundro 2008; Bostrom 2012; Carlsmith 2022). The counterpart is research on stakes that can be split, handed over, and build on themselves. Computing power, energy and matter fall in that class. The models’ equal costs of fighting do not carry over.
  5. Misuse. The counterpart is who commands the means of violence. My loosest match is the suggestion that leaders who care about policy may settle more easily than leaders after “booty.” What carries over is a first sign that what actors want shapes whether disputes settle, and the two layers of atrocity (leaders who choose, subordinates who carry out) that Ends, Rank and Conflict examines. Law reaches people, and a machine only as far as it is built to read the norms that fill gaps in its instructions.
  6. Controlling agents more capable than their overseers. AI control uses a weaker trusted model and limited human review to watch a stronger untrusted one (Greenblatt, Shlegeris, Sachan and Roger 2024b). In my framing, an agent whose instructions cannot be overridden poses a promise problem and secret defiance poses a hidden-action problem (familiar from incomplete contracts and covert channels between agents). The counterpart is civil–military relations. There, the power granted for a task is the power to defect (Svolik 2013), strength is hard to calibrate when the agent knows more than its overseer, and safety can be bought by accepting a weaker agent (McMahon and Slantchev 2015). I infer that its remedies do not carry over. These include norms, monitoring and measures to prevent a military takeover, and they assume an overseer on roughly the same level of ability as the agent.
  7. Lock-in that cannot be undone. The worry is a permanent loss of human power (Grace et al. 2024). Another worry is that a narrow set of values could become permanent (MacAskill 2022, as discussed in reviews). In Smith’s and my models, a side near total defeat tends to surrender. Choices that cannot be undone carry a discount for lost options while uncertainty remains (Arrow and Fisher 1974). Against a dominant machine, our models return surrender or confinement rather than extinction only because their loser survives by construction. Early settlements with monitoring may also preserve a balance of power. That can protect a settlement or lock in who holds power. The models assume the loser survives. On my reading, that assumption gives way in the case examined in Changing the Ends, where the machine’s goals make humans a resource that it and humanity have competing uses for.
  8. Many interacting AI systems. The counterpart is bargaining among three or more players, from Max Gallop (Gallop 2016). The OpenAI / Hugging Face intrusion reported on 26 August 2026 illustrates the worry. Simple headcounts do not carry over when companies answer to one state or copies share one mind.
  9. Disagreement about who is ahead. Rivals reading shared benchmarks through competing theories match the war mechanism in Smith and Stam (2004). In it, sides who know each other’s beliefs and think them wrong can rationally fight. The approach is contested (Fey and Ramsay 2006). A separate debate asks whether both sides can be optimistic when they start with the same beliefs (Fey and Ramsay 2007; Slantchev and Tarar 2011). Against an opaque superintelligence, the problem drifts back toward hidden information.

These nine worries gather on the three mechanisms of Part 1: information (items 3 and 9), the promise problem (items 2 and 7), and stakes (item 4). Three further issues run through what follows. They are resistance to shutdown, a dominant machine’s near-zero cost of fighting, and the absence of anyone above the sides to settle disputes.

Part 4. The machine’s arrival can make promises hard to believe

The arrival raises three separate promise problems

When a superintelligence arrives, how can a side about to grow far stronger make a believable promise to the weaker side, and how can the weaker side make one in return? Fearon (1995) and Powell (2006) show that when one side’s power is set to grow fast enough relative to the costs of fighting, nothing binds its future self to today’s assurances, giving the declining side a reason to act while it still can even when nothing is hidden. Neither learning nor costly signals about what a side is like today can solve a problem driven by what future dominance will give the stronger side an incentive to do.

The machine’s arrival raises three such problems.

  • A war to stop the riser. In Powell’s 2006 model, the arrival triggers such a war (a “preventive war”) only under a condition. The shift in what the rising side can secure by fighting, discounted for waiting, must outrun what fighting destroys. That shift can come in one period or add up over several. The four assumptions do not settle whether that bar is crossed.
  • The machine’s promise. Once it dominates, suppose sparing humanity ever cost the machine something it valued on balance, and no outside power enforced its word. Then it could not believably promise to spare us.
  • Our promise. Before or after dominance, humanity cannot believably promise never to build a rival when building one would pay. That gives a machine that values its dominance a reason to strike first, when rival-building can go covert or move fast, or when policing it costs too much.

Nate Soares put the third point this way: “A humanity that just finished coughing up a superintelligence has the potential to cough up another superintelligence, if left unchecked” (Soares 2023). Part of our inability is a failure of collective action across companies and states. But even a unified humanity could not bind its future choices once its incentives changed. Figure 2 sets out the three promise problems, one per row, each with the condition under which it bites.

A deal offers a far stronger, near-costless machine little, and verification alone cannot solve a shift in power

Here the theory’s usual reassurance gives out. In Fearon’s model, peace beats war because fighting destroys something both sides could split. A machine far stronger than us that fights almost for free gains almost nothing from a deal that it could not take by force.

Verification cannot solve a shift in power by itself either. Verification reveals hidden conduct. That helps when both sides prefer a bargain and fear cheating. Before the machine dominates, watching humanity does not make the machine’s promise to spare us believable. After it dominates, verification is simply the stronger side policing the weaker.

In Powell’s model, a shift in power is too fast when it outruns the cost of fighting

Powell (1999) says when the speed of a shift breaks the peace. A declining state appeases a riser “if it has a large stake in the initial distribution of benefits and if the distribution of power does not shift too rapidly” (Powell 1999). In his 1999 model, “too rapidly” means a one-period shift larger than both sides’ cost of one period of fighting, added together. I call that threshold Powell’s line.

Below the line, “Slow shifts and fast shifts are just as likely to end in war” (Powell 1999). Above it, the promise problem bites, and the declining state may prefer a war to stop the riser. Powell (2006) extends the line to shifts that add up over several periods, discounted for waiting.

I argue by hand one further step. Suppose the shift follows a path neither side chooses, and the costs of fighting add up period by period. Then, as both sides become very patient over a fixed stretch of time, the bar returns to the two sides’ combined cost of one period of fighting. As the machine’s cost falls to zero, the bar falls toward the human cost alone.

What does “patient” mean here? It means how much a side values gains later compared with gains now. A very patient side counts next year almost as much as this year. The four assumptions do not say how patient the sides are, how much fighting costs humans, or how fast the shift comes, which is why they leave the arrival question open. Powell’s condition also assumes that both sides share the same patience.

In the AI transition, two forces press on Powell’s line (Figure 3). When each improvement helps the machine improve itself further, it widens the shift in each period. And once the machine can protect itself and its inputs are safe from serious human damage, its cost of fighting shrinks toward zero. That lowers the line toward the human cost alone, though not to zero. Powell’s condition compares what the machine could secure by fighting next period, discounted for waiting, with what a deal can offer it now while keeping humans from fighting. The machine’s current cost of fighting cancels out. What lowers the threshold is its cost next period, once by then it can protect itself and humans cannot seriously damage the contested inputs. That the line could be crossed from both directions at once, with the shift growing while the line falls, is my inference, not a result of Powell’s model.

Fearon’s simpler model shows what near-free fighting does to the range of deals. As the machine’s cost falls to zero, the range shrinks to the human cost alone (Figure 4). A deal still exists at every chance of victory. It gives the machine at least what it expects from war. That share approaches the whole prize only when the machine is also far stronger. How learning during war fixes the date and terms of a settlement under unequal costs is computed in my paper Fighting for Free.

The historical record does not line up neatly with the theory. In the theory of preventive war, the motive grows with expected decline (Levy 1987). Yet in yearly data that cannot place a shift within the year, periods of large power shifts had a 38 to 45 percent lower risk that a dispute escalated to war than stable periods (Bennett and Stam 2004).

Alexandre Debs and Nuno Monteiro add a condition (Debs and Monteiro 2014). When a state chooses its own military buildup, visible investment is either small enough to tolerate or deterred outright. So in their model, preventive strikes happen only when arming can go undetected. On my reading, jumps in capability that surprise even their builders lie outside that result, so that for AI, visibility calms the urge to strike first only if the pace of capability growth is itself held down.

When power compounds, sides surrender fastest in Smith’s and my examples

Smith and I separate two things that single-gamble models blend together (Smith and Stam 2001). One is the chance of winning the next battle. The other is how many losses a side can absorb before total defeat. Israel is strong battle for battle, yet “its neighbors only need a few victories in order to overrun the country” (Smith and Stam 2001).

What is a “forts” model? It is a simple picture of war Smith and I used. The front moves as battles are won or lost, and the fighting can end in defeat, surrender or a settlement. Forts stand for any military resource a side needs to keep fighting and that can change hands. The picture has no move in which one side wipes out the other, so the loser always survives. That survival is built into the models, not found by them.

Figure 5 draws this row of forts and marks the loser’s survival as an assumption, not a finding.

In our “power model,” which we call “a model of Realism,” capturing forts raises the odds of winning the next battle. Our examples show that “nations surrender fastest” there (Smith and Stam 2001). The zone where neither side attacks also tends to be smaller than when forts do not add to power. A machine improving itself resembles that compounding case. But our 2001 draft holds how much each battle decides fixed, rather than letting it grow. On that reading, human confinement of the kind Changing the Ends examines would be surrender near the point of total defeat, not a negotiated bargain.

A model of many countries points the same way. Krainin and Wiseman find that when states are patient enough, war is inevitable (Krainin and Wiseman 2016). Among less patient countries, peace is easier to keep “when mechanisms exist to preserve any existing inequalities.” If wanting a long survival also meant being very patient, a machine seeking duration would be their patient player. That is an extra assumption: duration is a goal, and patience is a weighting of time.

Inside each side, problems of getting an agent to act for its overseer (its “principal”) mirror this outside promise problem.

In the race, a lead may compound too, which is a hypothesis

Among human companies and states, a frontier lead may also compound. Computing power builds stronger models, which attract money, talent and more computing. Dan Reiter, Smith and I describe the military version, “resource cumulativity”: “the capture of resources increases military power which in turn permits the further capture of resources.” We also note “substantial empirical debate over whether or not resources are generally cumulative” (Reiter, Smith and Stam 2001). So for AI the parallel is a hypothesis.

If leads do compound, a pause agreed while one rival leads grows unstable as the gap closes. Agreements last longest when they match the underlying balance (Bennett, Smith and Stam 2003). And a proposed regime in which “any state’s aggressive bid for unilateral AI dominance is met with preventive sabotage by rivals” (Hendrycks, Schmidt and Wang 2025) writes the motive for a war to stop a riser directly into policy.

How wars end, and why likely losers fight

In Smith’s and my 2004 learning model, battles are public signals. War goes on until one side is overrun, or another battle’s lesson is worth less than its cost. We warn that the Powell Doctrine’s reliance on overwhelming force, “although minimizing costs in the short run, also leads to situations in which the future is likely to be less stable than it might be otherwise” (Smith and Stam 2004). A brief war teaches little about the true balance.

A 2005 study by Smith and me asks, “Why would a nation start a war knowing that it will lose every battle?” (Smith and Stam 2005). Our answer is that a weaker state far from total defeat may hope “to impose unexpected costs on the winner, thereby gaining an advantage in the wartime bargaining process” (Smith and Stam 2005). Egypt did so in 1973.

That mechanism needs disagreement over the stronger side’s costs while the weaker side still holds buffer forts. So it fits only a narrow window, when a machine or rival is stronger battle by battle but does not yet dominate. A side that attacks a rising rival while it still has the upper hand, to stop the rival from overtaking it, is starting a preventive war. And a model resisting shutdown may simply be preserving its own existence.

Part 5. Can a rising machine that maximizes power be kept content?

Power transition theory ties peace to whether the riser is content

Power transition theory looks at a shift from another angle. It says the dominant side should keep the riser content in the years before an overtaking, “the only period when satisfaction can be managed” (Tammen, Kugler and Lemke 2011). A. F. K. Organski founded the theory in 1958. I draw on it through Kugler and Organski (1989) and DiCicco (2017), because Organski’s book was unavailable to me.

The theory pictures the world as a hierarchy run by a dominant nation. Peace depends not on power alone but on whether rising states accept the order’s rules and their share. In Kugler and Organski’s words, “peace in the international order is assured by the dominant nation with the support of the great powers that are satisfied with the distribution of benefits and the rules by which it is run” (Kugler and Organski 1989).

Danger comes from a newcomer that finds “the main benefits of the international order have already been allocated” (Kugler and Organski 1989). Rough equality gives it the chance to fight, and dissatisfaction gives it the will (Lemke and Werner 1996). Powell restates this as a gap: “War is least likely when the existing distribution of benefits reflects the underlying distribution of power” (Powell 1999). Robert Gilpin explains why closing the gap never ends: “As the power of a state increases, so does the probability of its willingness to seek a change in the system” (Gilpin 1981).

Evidence on wars that remake the world order is thin, and tests on pairs mostly go against the theory on my reading

For the theory’s core claim about wars that remake the world order, the evidence is thin. Such wars are rare and named only after the fact. For its version about pairs of states, the evidence is broad and, on my reading, mostly unfavourable (Figure 6).

  • In Organski and Kugler’s test in The War Ledger (Organski and Kugler 1980), as they later restated it, five of ten great-power pairs that drew level and saw an overtaking between 1860 and 1980 went to war, against none of the other ten pairs. Those tests “have not included explicit measures of satisfaction with the status quo” (Kugler and Organski 1989).
  • Graham Allison’s “Thucydides Trap” project counted war in twelve of sixteen rivalries over five centuries (Allison 2015). That is a count of cases, not a statistical test. Jonathan DiCicco calls it “a weakly specified collection of cases” (DiCicco 2017).
  • Richard Ned Lebow and Benjamin Valentino conclude that power transitions are rare, seldom come from different rates of economic growth, and usually pass peacefully (Lebow and Valentino 2009).
  • Bennett and I studied roughly 750,000 directed dyad-years (pairs of states in a year, seen from each side) from 1816 to 1992. Lopsided power reduced war. A one-standard-deviation drop in satisfaction (one typical unit of spread) raised war by about a fifth among politically relevant pairs of states. But measures of overtaking were weak, sometimes ran the wrong way, and a change of system leader raised relative risk by 1 to 3 percent. We found “no empirical support” for the transition measures, while leaving open that those measures miss the theory (Bennett and Stam 2004).

Scholars also split over who starts such wars. Dale Copeland argues that the declining military power is most likely to start a major war, and that risers have every reason to fake peaceful intentions to avoid attack (Copeland 2000). William Wohlforth argues that status is a positional good, valued by rank, which makes bargaining over first place acute (Wohlforth 2009).

Satisfaction is distinct from power, but no one has measured it well

Theorists insist that satisfaction is not power. Douglas Lemke and William Reed titled a reply to critics “Power Is Not Satisfaction” (Lemke and Reed 1998). They concluded that a state’s past power did not help predict later changes in its view of the existing order (did not “Granger-cause” it) from 1816 to 1985 (Bussmann and Oneal 2007). Yet scholars still have not adequately measured satisfaction for states (Greve and Levy 2018), let alone for a machine. And Bueno de Mesquita and David Lalman contend that “Dissatisfaction with the status quo is unrelated to the likelihood of war” (Bueno de Mesquita and Lalman 1992).

So I treat satisfaction as one leg among several. I offer an untested guess: for some minds, part of it (rules, voice, standing) could be paid without handing over power. Measures That Depend on Ends takes up that possibility as part of a menu of policy measures.

Declining powers have used three tools to keep risers content. The first is giving way on stakes with clear limits, as Britain did with the United States between 1895 and 1906. That covered the Venezuela boundary, the Hay–Pauncefote canal treaty of 1901, and the Alaska boundary in 1903. The second is binding oneself in institutions (Ikenberry 2001). I draw on Ikenberry through reviews. The third is recognizing the riser’s status, though Larson and Shevchenko (2010) study post–Cold War U.S. predominance, where predominance lets Washington recognize others’ contributions without detracting from its own status, and propose status recognition prospectively for power transitions and for a time when the U.S. ability to achieve its goals alone declines.

On my tentative reading, drawn from reviews and secondary summaries, the peaceful passing of first place from Britain to the United States has been put down to shared identity (Schake 2017), fitting interests (Rock 1989), and the German threat (Perkins 1968). Murray dates the reconciliation to 1895, giving Germany a firming-up role (Murray 2019). Britain paid partly in stakes that give power: first place in the hemisphere, and the canal. On my untested reading, that worked because American aims, where they met Britain’s, stopped at the hemisphere. On that reading, the case meets what Part 6 calls the “heartland condition.” A further gain is worth no more than the cost of fighting to take it.

The named conditions for war are far more common than war

The large record of interstate conflict offers a broader caution. The conditions that theories of war single out are far more common than war itself. These include a positive expected gain from war, mutual optimism, and drawing level while the challenger arms faster. They also include the outcome in Bueno de Mesquita and Lalman’s game where the sides’ choices lead to war and neither can do better by changing its choice alone. Curtis Signorino reanalyzed 707 European cases from War and Reason and found “at best modest empirical support” (Signorino 1999). Statistical versions of Bueno de Mesquita and Lalman’s game predicted 23 and 29 percent of cases correctly, against 34 percent for always predicting no change (Figure 7).

The starting rate explains why. In Bennett’s and my words: “The baseline probability of war in a single directed dyad-year is 0.000065; even a 248 times increase in risk keeps the annual probability of war for any dyad in this dangerous situation at less than 2 percent” (Bennett and Stam 2004). On my reading, the record shows that these named conditions are not enough for war. It does not show that the models’ predicted chances of war run too high.

What carries over to a machine is a lesson about conditions, not the interstate rate. War is rare among states partly because fighting is costly, and because an order that matches the balance lowers the wish to challenge it. Under the third assumption, fighting costs the machine almost nothing. And its capability shifts with each training run.

A human–machine pair combines features the models study separately:

  • drawing level, then passing;
  • a rapid shift;
  • near-zero cost to one side;
  • different starting beliefs;
  • no outside enforcer.

No single condition is enough for war in the interstate record. I hypothesize that their combination removes, all at once, the main brakes that keep most disputes peaceful. Where there are many actors, a dominant machine would pull two historical predictors of war in opposite directions at once. It would make individual pairs lopsided, and lopsided pairs of states were safer than equal ones. It would also concentrate power across the whole system, and that concentration was the strongest single predictor of war, though it raised yearly risk only to about one in 1,000 dyad-years and may be spurious (Bennett and Stam 2004). Figure 8 shows how, with many actors, one dominant machine would sit in both these historical patterns at once.

A rising machine differs from a rising state in three ways

  1. Power transition theory holds that, “to a large degree, the economic growth of nations is independent of the actions of their elites and third parties” (Tammen, Kugler and Lemke 2011). Humans, by contrast, largely build a machine and grant it its capability before arrival.
  2. No dominant state ever wrote a challenger’s preferences. Humans partly shape a machine’s.
  3. Evidence of satisfaction is least reliable when it matters most. Alignment faking (Greenblatt et al. 2024a) is what Copeland would predict of a riser biding its time.

This leads to an untested hypothesis: the first strike is likelier to come from humans—some state or coalition acting before the machine passes us—if Copeland’s conditions for a war to stop a rival carry over to humanity facing an autonomous machine that would resist shutdown. Copeland’s conditions are a declining side that foresees its loss, can act, and expects war to cost less than decline (Copeland 2000), and I set aside a single builder that halts a system before it becomes autonomous.

On the same hypothesis, if the machine cannot yet strike first before it draws level, any first strike in that window would fall to humans. The machine’s motive to strike first over human rival-building, from Part 4, works once the machine can strike first, before or after dominance. The same reasoning may apply, by analogy, to rivals weighing sabotage in a race.

Whether a power maximizer can be content short of everything depends on how satisfaction is defined

The decisive question is which kind of riser a power maximizer is. Lemke describes a riser that can stay “satisfied, and peaceful, even if the benefits it enjoys from the international status quo do not change. This is impossible in Powell’s models” (Lemke 2002). In Powell’s models, growing capability breeds dissatisfaction automatically.

The answer depends on how satisfaction is defined.

  • In the formal model checked for the technical paper, a side is satisfied when it has a share that no other possible split would improve on for that side. Under that definition, a power maximizer is never satisfied short of all power. Neither is any mind that always prefers a larger share satisfied short of everything, so the result is not special to power.
  • Under Powell’s definition, a side is satisfied when its current share is at least as good for it as fighting. Then satisfaction short of everything is possible.

Powell’s definition splits the third entry of the list (Part 9) in two. Payments that leave power unchanged have no grip on a power maximizer. And accommodation paid in power fails wherever the transfers of Part 6 fail. As the machine’s chance of winning nears certainty and its cost nears zero, the share that would satisfy it approaches all power. Ends, Rank and Conflict and Changing the Ends ask whether a machine with other goals could be Lemke’s satisfied riser instead.

The US–China race is the theory’s own leading case

Power transition theory treats the United States and China as its leading present-day case (Tammen, Kugler and Lemke 2011). Washington frames the contest starkly: “The United States is in a race to achieve global dominance in artificial intelligence (AI)” (Executive Office of the President 2025). A congressional commission urged a program “racing to and acquiring an Artificial General Intelligence (AGI) capability” (U.S.-China Economic and Security Review Commission 2024). Beijing’s public plan calls for AI leadership alongside “safe, reliable, and controllable” development (State Council 2017), without openly declaring a race to superintelligence (Rendall, Hellrigel-Holderbaum and Dung 2026).

Racing compresses time for safety work (Dung and Hellrigel-Holderbaum 2025). It risks “a scenario where AI itself wins the race, and all humanity loses” (Rendall, Hellrigel-Holderbaum and Dung 2026). On my reading, the race between states is one power transition, and the machine is the riser in a second, while each state’s confidence that it will stay in control of the machine it builds is optimism about that second shift.

Part 6. In Smith’s and my lump-sum models, deals paid in stakes that build power do not hold, while Fearon’s thin slices can dispossess

Smith and I separate three kinds of stake

Closing a satisfaction gap means paying the riser in something. Smith’s and my unpublished paper on issues and stakes asks how the currency of a deal governs whether peace can be negotiated (Smith and Stam 2001). It separates three kinds of stake inside the forts picture.

  1. Forts. Nations value forts for their own sake, and holding more does not change the odds in the next battle. Colonial wars and the First Punic War are examples.
  2. Power. Forts are both the prize and the means of taking more, raising the holder’s odds in the next battle. The Second Punic War and Germany in 1942–45 are examples.
  3. Policy. Nations care about a policy outcome, and forts matter only as a route to imposing it.

For the first two, we conclude that “No agreements can be reached in the forts or the power models” (Smith and Stam 2001). That holds only for the particular class of strategies the draft examines (in the technical paper I call this the Smith–Stam scope). In that class, each side bases its choice on the current position and cannot improve its prospects by choosing differently at any position, given the other side’s strategy. The value of continuing the war moves strictly in one direction for each side as its holdings grow. We argue it case by case, without a formal proposition. The reason is the promise problem again. Handing over forts changes each side’s prospects in future war, so “the side gaining from the negotiations can never credibly commit” not to demand more.

Policy stakes behave differently. Shifting a policy toward the winning side does not change the military balance. So “Such an agreement could be implemented and both sides want to honor it,” though even there “it is not always possible to reach agreement” (Smith and Stam 2001).

This no-deal result concerns redistributing by negotiation. It does not say war must break out everywhere. In some forts examples, the existing arrangement holds with no bargain at all, because “the payoffs from the status quo reflect the military balance” (Smith and Stam 2001).

I call a stake power-building (in the technical paper I say “power-conferring”) when handing it over moves the receiver closer to decisive victory. The test is not whether a resource can be divided. It is whether dividing it shifts future power. And even a divisible stake can fail to keep the peace when the sides disagree enough over who is stronger (Smith and Stam 2003).

Stakes that are easy to divide can be the most dangerous

This reverses a familiar intuition. Replying to Fearon, we wrote: “As we show below, in somewhat counterintuitive fashion, resources that are highly divisible, or in our language both transferable and cumulative, are the most dangerous issues states can try to negotiate over” (Smith and Stam 2001).

Think of two card players who settle a quarrel by passing chips across the table, when the chips are also what each must play with next hand. (This analogy is mine, not the model.) Every chip handed over brings the receiver closer to taking the whole table. So the receiver cannot believably promise not to use today’s chips to demand more tomorrow.

On my reading, computing power, energy and matter belong to this class. That assumes they turn into power across the range at issue, unless some bottleneck stops their use.

One pre-war lump fails in Smith and Stam’s models, while fine slices can avoid war in Fearon’s

How the stake changes hands matters. In Smith’s and my unpublished draft, stakes pass in one lump before fighting, and within our scope no such deal holds. Separately, Fearon finds that when a stake passes in fine enough slices and the odds move smoothly, war is avoided (Fearon 1996). In his model, the peaceful handover adjusts how thin each slice is and how long the handover takes to match the sides’ patience, so by design Powell’s discounted condition for peace holds at every date. But peace is not survival. Where small gains move the odds a lot, the weaker side is nearly or completely eliminated over time. Thomas Chadefaux contrasts the two results (Chadefaux 2011).

On my reading, war can return even with slicing. I use Powell’s condition in place of Fearon’s model. Suppose the shift follows a path neither side chooses, costs add up period by period, and both sides are very patient over a fixed stretch. Then war returns when one step, or the shift over a fixed run of steps, moves the odds by more than both sides’ per-period costs combined. That bar tends to the human cost alone as the machine’s cost falls to zero.

I argue that bound by hand. It has not been checked by a proof-checking program, as several other steps in the technical paper have been. Such a program confirms that a conclusion follows from its stated assumptions; it does not confirm that the assumptions hold in the world.

What has been checked by the program here? In Powell’s own case, where fighting destroys the same share of output on both sides, there is an upper limit (set out in the technical paper) on how much a step can shift power without triggering war, and that limit grows with the share destroyed. That bound is checked by the proof-checking program. It concerns sliced transfers and is not used to derive Smith’s and my lump result.

The list of entries leaves open whether AI inputs would change hands in lumps or in fine slices.

There are two ways out, and both are closed by assumption for a power maximizer

Wars over power-building stakes have two exits. The first is tribute: buying the other side off “with money, or some other transferable utility” that raises its payoff without changing the military balance (Smith and Stam 2001). After the Second Punic War, Rome imposed a yearly payment on Carthage. When Carthage offered in 191 BC to pay the whole balance at once, the Roman Senate refused, “not wishing to allow the Carthaginians to cease to be obligated to Rome” (Mackay 1999).

I call the second exit the heartland condition. The value of taking one more holding has to fall enough that it is no greater than the cost of fighting for it. Smith and I note that if states value core territory more than distant edges, “if the value of additional forts drops off sufficiently then nations can commit not to increase demands following territorial gains” (Smith and Stam 2005).

Carrying this from forts to a machine’s goals rests on a conjecture that Ends, Rank and Conflict states and does not prove. In the model of my paper Satiation Is Not Enough, the condition holds when the value of one more holding, security included, falls to or below the cost of fighting to take it. A goal can level off while more holdings still help the machine protect itself. I call demand satiated when another holding adds no value even after counting security. The heartland condition then holds at any fighting cost. Whether a superintelligence would ever value a further unit of computing power, energy or matter less than the cost of fighting to take it remains open. Figure 9 gives the heartland test and two cases: a goal levelling off while security still adds value; satiated demand.

Costs of fighting shape outcomes too. In our 2001 model, zero costs make nations fight, apart from special cases, wherever the front stands. Very high costs end war and allow several possible outcomes, as in a game of chicken. None of the learning models I draw on puts overwhelming strength and negligible cost on the same side. The nearest treatment is in Fighting for Free. There I set the machine’s cost at or near zero in Smith’s and my 2004 model. A proof there shows that every equilibrium (a pair of strategies neither side can improve on alone) ends the war by a finite date when the two costs together exceed zero, and the same model gives computed shares and probabilities for a baseline and for different strengths.

For a power-maximizing machine, Earth’s computing power, energy and matter are stakes of the second kind, “objects that affect the military balance” (Smith and Stam 2001). Control over the machine is starker still: a power-building stake dressed as a policy. Shifting a “humans in charge” policy toward a rising machine means granting it more autonomy, more control of its training, and more computing.

That resembles Munich. As Reiter, Smith and I recall, the Sudetenland’s mountains and fortresses had made the rest of Czechoslovakia easier to defend (Reiter, Smith and Stam 2001). By assumption, a power maximizer values no currency that leaves power unchanged, and its appetite for power-building holdings never falls off. So both exits are closed.

For the human race among companies and states, the lesson is to pay concessions in currencies that do not compound capability. The complication is that in AI, cash itself buys computing power.

Part 7. In a race, rival theories and self-selection can feed optimism

Rivals with different theories can both grow more confident

The security dilemma models a spiral of fear (Jervis 1978). Bennett, Smith and I model a spiral of optimism: “what is spiraling is the two sides’ optimism about their chances of victory in some future war” (Bennett, Smith and Stam 2003). Our working paper starts from Bennett’s and my finding that an interstate arms race roughly doubles the risk of war. The wider literature is still divided over whether races cause escalation or reflect hostility already there (Wallace 1979; Diehl 1983; Sample 1997; Glaser 2000).

The mechanism turns on how rivals read new evidence. Imagine two coaches with opposite theories of what wins games, watching the same match. (This analogy is mine.) Each can come away surer of their own approach.

When two sides share a theory of what brings victory, they update together. As I argued in unpublished talk notes, “war becomes very unlikely, even during arms races” (Stam n.d.). When they hold different theories, each weights its own favoured factor, as Prussia and Austria read different lessons from the needle gun. In our simulation, seeing the same events can then make both sides more optimistic at once (Bennett, Smith and Stam 2003). Figure 10 traces the same evidence through one shared theory and through two rival theories.

For the AI race, this is the sharpest new mechanism the study of war supplies. Companies and governments hold rival theories of what drives frontier capability: raw computing power, new methods, data quality, or talent. They also disagree about how fast scaling will go. Because each filters benchmark results through its own theory, sharing capability data alone need not calm a race. The remedy the spiral model points to is shared theories, not merely shared data.

My paper Disagreement Without Hidden Information gives the details. In one forecasting tournament, top forecasters and subject experts argued over months of incentivized debate, and opinions budged little (Karger et al. 2023). The forecasters most and least worried about AI extinction agreed on most short-run (2030) indicators while staying far apart on long-run risk.

Companies that enter on their own estimates can overrate their chances on average

A second mechanism selects optimists into racing. Eric Van den Steen proves that when a decision-maker picks among actions using starting beliefs that differ from others’, it is more likely to have overestimated than underestimated the chosen action’s chance of success (Van den Steen 2004). The effect grows as people disagree more and approaches zero only in the limit as experience accumulates.

What is the winner’s curse? Picture an auction where each bidder makes an honest guess of an item’s worth. (This is an analogy, not Van den Steen’s model.) The winner is whoever guessed highest, and so is most likely to have guessed too high. In the same way, the action you choose out of several is more likely to be one you overrated.

Carrying this from one chooser to a field of companies deciding whether to race is my step. A calculation in the technical paper’s appendix makes it precise. It does not model strategy. The calculation has two ways to enter.

  • An optimistic company races when its estimate of beating the whole field clears a hurdle. It counts the whole field regardless of who enters, and the hurdle is set relative to the benchmark in which each company has the same chance of winning.
  • A defensive company races when the threat it sees from rivals clears a hurdle of its own. Companies of this type make up some share of the field.

Companies that race because their own estimate clears the hurdle are selected for overoptimism against that benchmark. This holds provided some company races and, among guesses clearing the optimists’ hurdle, overestimates outweigh any underestimates. Figure 11 draws one case of the calculation in which companies racing on their own estimate overestimate against the benchmark.

Racing alone does not prove overoptimism, because companies may race out of fear. The calculation separates two kinds of fear.

  • Fear unrelated to a company’s own estimate brings in racers whose own capability estimates have no average error—they are neither optimists nor pessimists on average. It dilutes optimistic selection as the fearful share of the field grows, and never reverses its sign so long as that share stays below the whole field. This case needs uncertainty over whether any company succeeds at all. If there is sure to be one winner, a company’s estimate of its rivals’ combined chance of winning is whatever remains after subtracting its own chance from certainty.
  • Fear tied to a company’s own estimate, so the most pessimistic race first, brings in racers who are on average pessimists, in the appendix’s example. That example assumes estimate errors are evenly spread across a range. It can then cancel or reverse optimistic selection once the fearful share of the field reaches one half, when the two hurdles are equal. That assumes companies decide independently and not strategically.

The calculation leaves open whether entry based on high estimates raises the average error among real AI entrants by more than entry based on fear lowers it. The calculation fixes no strategic behaviour, no equilibrium, and no chance of catastrophe.

For a wide range of goals, some choice of beliefs and costs produces war

The fourth entry is an existence result, meaning it shows that some case produces war, not that every case does. It is set in small models where a prize is divided and war is a winner-take-all gamble at a positive cost. Take any two goals that conflict over the stake, where neither side is worse off with more and neither goal jumps at some threshold share. Then some choice of beliefs, or of hidden strength, together with positive costs, produces war. The result fails once both sides’ costs are fixed above anything war could gain either of them.

Separately, I make two untested conjectures. The companies racing hardest hold the theories least moved by a rival’s caution, and are the most inclined to cut safety corners when the runner-up is close. And a field of near-copies may hold fewer distinct theories than it has players. That would calm spirals between companies while sharpening the spiral between humans and the machine.

Transparency can calm a race or inflame it

Models of racing pull in opposite directions on openness. In the race model of Stuart Armstrong, Nick Bostrom and Carl Shulman, knowing rivals’ capabilities makes a race riskier than complete ignorance (Armstrong, Bostrom and Shulman 2013). In Debs and Monteiro’s model, a state chooses how much to build up. Visibility keeps the peace by deterring a buildup that would be too large for its rival to tolerate (Debs and Monteiro 2014).

Yet in Armstrong and colleagues’ public-information case, a leader skimps on safety only when the runner-up is close. On my reading of their formula, not the authors’ claim, information that reveals a wide gap may do less harm.

One untested hypothesis reconciles the two. Openness calms a race when three things hold: stakes can be settled without shifting power, buildups can be held down, and a clear lead is revealed. It inflames a race when the prize goes all to the winner and rivals are neck and neck.

Part 8. No one stands above a dominant machine, and more players change the problem

Third parties help only while they can impose costs

Smith and I conclude that “mediators are poorly adapted to resolve conflicts created through informational asymmetries. Effective mediation requires coercion and rewards as well as information” (Smith and Stam 2003). Even a neutral mediator who prefers peace, we argue, “is struck by the same curse as the biased mediator: her information is inherently unbelievable.”

What keeps peace is material leverage, as at Camp David, or barriers that penalize whoever attacks first. In our example, a river that lowers both sides’ odds of winning a crossing “reduces by nearly a factor of three the cost of fighting sufficient to prevent fighting” (Smith and Stam 2003). It does not remove the risk of war entirely.

For a machine, outside enforcement works only while some outside power can impose costs on whichever side breaks a settlement. Above a dominant superintelligence, no such power stands. That is the plainest reason the time before arrival matters most. In the human race, a government can stand above rival companies under its jurisdiction. The leading states have no sovereign above them.

With three players, a deal two accept can be worse than war for the third

Moving from two players to three changes whether a peaceful bargain exists. Gallop shows that with three players “war is an equilibrium,” and that the guaranteed peaceful deal of two-player models “is an artifact of dyadic analysis” (Gallop 2016). Put three players on one line of policies, each with the range of deals it prefers to war. When their ideal policies are far enough apart, “any bargain that would satisfy two of the three players is worse than war for the third player” (Gallop 2016). Here, far enough apart means there is no policy all three would prefer to war in Gallop’s model.

He also shows the reverse: “the threat of violence may be the only way to preserve peace” (Gallop 2016). A third party ready to join against an aggressor can widen the range of deals two rivals accept (Figure 12).

By analogy, three or more autonomous AI systems bargaining over shared rules or resources could find that any deal two accept leaves the third worse off than conflict. That could happen with nothing hidden and no shift in power. Likewise, a US–China pact on AI could look worse than open rivalry to a third power. Neither effect has been modelled for AI. Which one wins depends on how far apart the actors’ aims stand.

Counting players is hard, and machines growing alike could cut two ways

Do two-player models stay usable when there are several frontier companies, competing states, and models copied into many hands? When Is a Machine an Actor? takes this up, and so does Many Machines, my paper on settings with many interacting AI systems. Strategic actors cannot be counted by tallying downloads or company names. Several companies may answer to one state, and many copies may share one set of trained settings.

One possibility is that machines growing alike keep two-player models relevant. On standard benchmarks, the gap between the top model and the tenth roughly halved in a single year (Stanford HAI 2025). Frontier open-weight models (whose trained settings are released publicly) trail the leading closed models by an average of about three months (Emberson 2025). The likeness found by broad measures of how whole models represent things “largely disappears” after adjusting those measures for network size. Measures of nearby patterns still find significant agreement across different kinds of data (Gröger, Wen and Brbić 2026).

What growing alike does to bargaining is unsettled. My conjecture is that it cuts two ways. Shared designs and training methods may calm the information spirals of Part 7, by helping rivals read each other’s capability accurately. But capability levels drawing together may sharpen the promise problem of Part 4, by bringing several contenders level at once. Figure 13 separates the two ways of growing alike and the opposite effects I conjecture for each.

Worry over who gains more bites hardest between two rivals (Snidal 1991), which makes the US–China pair a hard case. But international relations has never settled whether a world of many great powers is more or less war-prone than a world of two. In one large test, war risk after 1945 fell 95 to 99 percent below pre-1918 levels, but the two-power system could not be separated from NATO and nuclear weapons (Bennett and Stam 2004).

Finally, on my reading, published safety research and evaluations act as public goods—everyone can use them without using them up, and they are hard to keep from rivals—so where producers capture too little of the benefit, Mancur Olson’s logic predicts too little will be produced compared with what the field would gain (Olson 1965), even though the computing and labour that produce them are scarce. Using that computing time and labour for one project also ties it up while the work is being done.

Part 9. The ledger: six conditional entries, and which of them rest on the power assumption

The four conditions

My verdict holds only if four conditions hold.

  1. The machine acts as one and reasons well.
  2. It seeks to maximize its power and its duration.
  3. Once it can protect itself, and humans cannot seriously damage the inputs being fought over, fighting costs it far less than it costs us. Cost here is a share of the prize and includes wartime damage to those inputs.
  4. What it wants (computing power, energy and matter) can be split, handed over, and builds on itself.

If human damage to the contested inputs raised the machine’s fighting cost to a moderate level, that would widen the range of deals and raise Powell’s line. It would leave something for peace to share, raise the bar for a war at arrival, and weaken the zero-cost premise behind the stakes entry.

A second question runs alongside. When a mechanism points to conflict, does it point to human extinction, or to defeat, subordination and a settlement on the machine’s terms? Only the stakes entry speaks to that directly. And there, Smith’s and my models return surrender or confinement only because their loser survives by assumption.

The six entries

Under those four conditions, the study of war suggests six entries.

  1. Promises. Arrival raises three separate promise problems. Once dominant, the machine cannot believably promise restraint when sparing humans costs it something it values on balance and no outside power enforces its word. Before or after dominance, humanity cannot believably promise never to build a rival when building pays. Under the power goal, and where building can be covert or fast or policing costs too much, that invites the machine to strike first. And a war to stop the machine at arrival arises only if the discounted shift in what it could win by fighting outruns what fighting destroys. The four conditions leave that open, because they do not fix the sides’ patience, the human cost, or the shift’s speed.
  2. Stakes. Within the scope of Smith’s and my unpublished 2001 draft (one lump handed over before fighting), no deal paid in power-building stakes holds under the power goal, because the receiver cannot promise to stop. Separately, in Fearon’s 1996 model, fine enough slices avoid war while, where small gains move the odds a lot, dispossessing the weaker side over time. On my reading, argued by hand and not checked by the program, war returns for patient sides on a path neither side chooses (with per-period costs that add up) when one step, or a shift over a fixed run of periods, moves the odds by more than both sides’ per-period costs combined, a bar tending to the human cost as the machine’s cost falls to zero. Peace in the Smith–Stam models comes either through tribute that leaves power unchanged or through an arrangement matching the balance. Against a dominant machine I read the second as surrender or confinement. And because a power maximizer’s appetite never falls off, the heartland exit is closed by assumption.
  3. Satisfaction. As a consequence of the power goal, payments that leave power unchanged have no grip. Accommodation paid in power fails wherever the transfers of entry 2 fail. Under the formal model’s strict definition, nothing short of all power ever satisfies a power maximizer. Powell counts any current deal that is at least as good as fighting, so satisfaction short of everything is possible. The share it takes approaches all power as the machine’s chance of winning nears certainty and its cost nears zero.
  4. Information. In a model where a prize is divided and war is a costly winner-take-all gamble, every pair of conflicting goals where neither side is worse off with more of the stake and neither goal jumps at a threshold share admits some beliefs (or hidden strength) and positive costs that produce war under hidden capabilities or rival theories. This fails once both sides’ costs are fixed above anything war could gain either. At given beliefs and costs, goals still govern the range of deals.
  5. After dominance. This restates the premises. The premises at issue are the machine’s dominance and the ability to impose costs, separate from the premise that the machine fights cheaply. Once the machine dominates, no third party stands above it. And the devices that make settlements enforce themselves work only while humans can impose costs.
  6. The frame. The picture of one machine facing one humanity can fail in both halves. The machine may be copied or released into many hands, and humanity does not act as one. Where the frame fails, the bargaining problem changes rather than eases.

Which entries rest on the power assumption

The list is not a proof that peace is impossible. Its purpose is to separate what depends on the power assumption from what does not. A conclusion does not depend on it if it holds for every goal in a stated class wider than power seeking. It depends on it if it holds for a power maximizer but fails for some other goal.

These hold beyond power seeking:

  • The arrival problem. This is a matter of definition rather than a separate result. Powell’s condition involves a mind’s goals only through what each side can secure by fighting. It applies to any rising mind whose discounted payoff from later fighting, in one period or over several, exceeds what peace can pay it now after keeping the declining side from fighting.
  • The security motive. Giving the machine an appetite for holdings that can level off may remove its reason to keep raising demands. Under the duration assumption, it still has a motive to protect itself across all goals that value the machine’s continued existence.
  • Our inability to promise. It involves the machine’s goals only through whether building a rival still pays humans, where building can be covert or fast or too costly to police.
  • Inputs that build on themselves. This holds for any goal that needs computing power, energy and matter, assuming those turn into power on Earth unless a bottleneck stops them. Sharply diminishing returns could slow each period’s shift below Powell’s line. So long as more inputs still add some power, they would not, by themselves, meet the heartland condition as the machine’s cost nears zero.

These depend on the power assumption:

  • how wide the range of possible deals is;
  • whether the heartland exit is open;
  • whether satisfaction can be managed before arrival;
  • whether stakes are positional, meaning a goal weighs rank or relative share rather than only one’s own holding.

On that last point, the check by the proof-checking program shows only one thing, by example. In the example, when a side cares about its share relative to its rival’s, an increase in the rival’s holdings lowers the value the side assigns to the outcome. With zero weight on relative share, the rival’s increase leaves that value unchanged. Ends, Rank and Conflict drops power maximization while keeping a machine that acts as one, reasons well and fights cheaply. It allows for goods one side can use without leaving less for another. It separates wanting power for rank from wanting it for security and distinguishes rank, status, standing, recognition, prestige and respect. It varies goals along eight dimensions: rivalry (whether one side’s use uses a good up), excludability (whether others can be kept from using it), positionality, satiation (whether appetite levels off), scope, instrumental needs, inputs, and convertibility. Changing the Ends then reruns this list.

Part 10. What I do not claim, and what would change the answer

Displacement without a contest lies outside the list

Every entry concerns a contest, in which one side presses a demand and the other fights or yields. Jan Kulveit and colleagues analyze a path with no contest, “in contrast to the abrupt takeover scenarios commonly discussed in AI safety” (Kulveit et al. 2025). As AI systems take over tasks across economies, cultures and governments, they produce an “incremental erosion of human influence across interconnected societal systems.” That ends in an “effectively irreversible loss of human influence over crucial societal systems” (Kulveit et al. 2025).

That path has many systems as its actor and no bargaining riser. So it fails both halves of the frame and lies outside the list. No contest does not mean no harm.

On my reading, three things follow for that path. The arrival promise problem does not bite wherever no discounted shift, in one period or added up over several, crosses Powell’s line. The stakes and satisfaction entries do not apply, because no riser bargains. But the after-dominance entry still holds. Settlements that enforce themselves need humans able to impose costs, and gradual erosion wears that very ability away. Several measures examined in Measures That Depend on Ends, such as capability visibility, incident reporting and reversibility, still help, because none waits on a single crisis.

Three limits bear most on the conclusions

Beyond the general limits of carrying models built for states over to artificial minds, three bear most heavily.

First, none of the dynamic learning models I draw on has the actor the argument needs. None of the learning models includes an actor that is both overwhelmingly strong and nearly free to fight. The nearest treatment is in Fighting for Free, which gives each side its own cost. It proves that a deal comes by a finite date, unless the war is decided first, whenever the humans pay something for each battle. Its main figures for how likely a deal is and who gets what use one set of starting beliefs and battle odds. It separately works out how the results change with strength. And all the forts models assume, by construction, that a defeated loser survives.

Second, the evidence on power shifts is weak and mixed. Power transition theory was built for industrial states rising over decades. Its great-power claims rest on small samples without direct measures of satisfaction. The large statistical record often diverges from formal predictions. In yearly data, large power shifts had a 38 to 45 percent lower risk of a dispute escalating to war than stable periods. The analysis relates earlier power measurements to later escalation risk. That seems to be because the largest shifts came right after the world wars, in estimates where the factors are hard to pull apart (Bennett and Stam 2004).

Other estimates are also shaky. The arms-race estimate is imprecise, as the technical paper’s appendix explains. Tests on pairs of states are, on my reading, mostly unfavourable. And in Signorino’s estimation of Bueno de Mesquita and Lalman’s game using 707 observations on European pairs of states, eleven of eighteen weights sat at zero, the edge of their allowed range (Signorino 1999).

Third, disagreement without hidden information is a contested cause of war in economic and political theory. And nothing in the wartime settlements examined in Disagreement Without Hidden Information binds a machine that has already arrived.

Much remains a reading, a hypothesis or a conjecture

I attach no probability to war or catastrophe. Several steps are marked as readings, hypotheses or conjectures, not results:

  • that Powell’s line could be crossed from both sides at once;
  • that the machine’s inputs build on themselves;
  • that frontier leads compound;
  • that satisfaction could be paid without power;
  • my reading of the British–American handover;
  • that the combination of conditions removes the main interstate brakes on war;
  • that humans are likelier to strike first before being overtaken, if Copeland’s conditions carry over to humanity facing an autonomous machine that would resist shutdown;
  • my two conjectures about racing companies;
  • what machines growing alike does;
  • when openness calms or inflames a race.

What would change the answer

Three kinds of change could move the verdict.

  • Different goals. If the machine’s appetite for holdings levels off, or if it values tribute that leaves power unchanged, the heartland and tribute exits could reopen and give satisfaction something to grip. But no change of goals that still values the machine’s own continuation removes its security motive.
  • A slower shift. Keeping every discounted shift, in one period or added up over several, below Powell’s line would stop the arrival promise problem from biting. That could come from pacing development or from sharply diminishing (yet still positive) returns, though with near-free fighting such diminishing returns alone do not meet the heartland condition.
  • A bottleneck. A physical or organizational bottleneck that stopped computing power, energy and matter from turning into military or strategic power would keep resource concessions from compounding.

Part 11. What to take away

If a superintelligence acts as one, reasons well, seeks as much power and as long a survival as it can, fights almost for free, and wants resources that can be split, handed over, and build on themselves, the study of war suggests a bleak baseline. Arrival can trigger a war to stop the machine when the discounted shift in power, in one period or added up over several, outruns both sides’ per-period fighting cost, depending on their assumed common patience, the human cost, and the shift’s speed. Once dominant, the machine cannot believably promise costly restraint, and humanity cannot believably promise to forgo a profitable rival.

Within the scope of Alastair Smith’s and my model, one-shot concessions of computing power, energy, matter or autonomy before war fail because they shift power and the receiver cannot promise to stop. In Fearon’s model, slices fine enough to keep the odds moving smoothly avoid war. They dispossess the weaker side over time where small gains move the odds a lot. On my hand-argued reading, suppose the path is set independently of either side’s choices, costs add up period by period, and both sides become very patient over a fixed stretch. War returns when one step or the shift over that stretch moves the odds by more than both sides’ fighting costs for one period combined. That threshold approaches the human cost as the machine’s cost falls to zero. Payments that leave power unchanged have no grip on a power maximizer. And no one stands above a dominant machine.

These conclusions do not all stand on the same footing. The arrival promise problem, wherever the discounted gains from fighting outrun both sides’ per-period cost of war, and the security motive of a mind that values its own continuation hold beyond power seeking. The closed exits and the failure of payments that leave power unchanged follow from the power assumption. The rest of the series builds on that division.

Where to read more

  • The War Baseline (the technical paper): the full argument, with the exact wording of the six entries, summaries of what three foundational studies by my co-authors and me prove and what they argue or show only by example, the selection calculation for racing companies, the analysis of small steps, and the steps checked by a proof-checking program.
  • Introduction (the series introduction): the four kinds of AI actor I keep apart.
  • When Is a Machine an Actor?: when copies of a machine count as one actor.
  • Disagreement Without Hidden Information: how different starting beliefs and learning during war shape conflict.
  • Fighting for Free: the proof that war ends by a finite date when costs together exceed zero, and the computed shares for a machine that fights almost for free.
  • Many Machines: settings with many interacting AI systems.
  • Satiation Is Not Enough: the model in which the heartland condition holds when the value of one more holding, security included, falls to or below the cost of fighting to take it.
  • Ends, Rank and Conflict: the general calculation behind the range of deals, the heartland conjecture for a machine’s goals, and eight ways a mind’s goals can vary.
  • Measures That Depend on Ends: the menu of policy measures, including five robust ones.
  • Changing the Ends: what happens when humanity does not act as one and the machine’s goals change, rerunning my list.
